text:
The Long Way Home: Apollo 13

On the afternoon of April 11, 1970, a Saturn V rocket lifted from Florida carrying three men toward the Moon. By then, Americans had landed on the Moon twice, and the public had begun to treat the journeys as routine. Network television had even stopped carrying the astronauts' broadcasts live. Apollo 13 would change that within three days.

The crew was led by Jim Lovell, a veteran of three earlier spaceflights who was about to make his fourth. Fred Haise, a rookie, would pilot the lunar module. The third seat was supposed to belong to Ken Mattingly, but a few days before launch doctors learned he had been exposed to German measles, and he was grounded. Jack Swigert, his backup, took his place with almost no time to spare. The crew named their command ship Odyssey and their landing craft Aquarius. Their destination was the Fra Mauro highlands, a rugged region they hoped to explore on foot.

The first two days went smoothly. The crew settled into the long outbound coast, and the spacecraft behaved. On the evening of April 13, about 55 hours into the flight and some 200,000 miles from Earth, Mission Control asked the crew to stir the supercold liquid oxygen and hydrogen tanks in the service module, a routine step that keeps the contents from stratifying. Swigert flipped the switches. A little over a minute later, the crew heard a loud bang and felt the ship shudder.

Swigert said the words that became famous in a slightly altered form: "Okay, Houston, we've had a problem here." Lovell repeated it a moment later. Warning lights flickered. Voltage on one main electrical bus dropped. Then Lovell looked out the window and saw gas streaming into space. Oxygen was venting from the service module, the unpressurized section behind the crew cabin that held their power and air supply.

The cause lay in a chain of small mistakes made years earlier. An oxygen tank had been dropped slightly during handling in 1968, damaging an internal fill tube. During ground testing, its heater switches had been exposed to a higher voltage than they were built for and had fused shut, which nobody noticed. When Swigert turned on the tank's stirring fans, bare wires with damaged insulation sparked inside a tank filled with pure oxygen. The tank burst, and the blast crippled a second one. Within hours, two of the spacecraft's three fuel cells had died and the oxygen was gone. Without it, the command module could not make electricity or breathable air for much longer.

In Houston, flight controllers pored over their consoles. Gene Kranz and his team realized the landing was out of the question. The goal changed from reaching the Moon to getting three men home alive. The answer lay in Aquarius. The lunar module was designed to carry two men to the surface and back for a couple of days. Now it would serve as a lifeboat for three people for four. The crew shut down Odyssey to save its remaining battery power for the final descent and crawled into the lunar module.

The next question was how to turn around. The ship was on a path that would swing around the Moon and return toward Earth, but not on a precise course, and it would take too long. Engineers decided against a direct turnaround, which would have required using the damaged service module engine. Instead they chose to fly around the far side of the Moon and then fire the lunar module's descent engine to speed the trip home. That burn, performed after the ship emerged from behind the Moon, shortened the return considerably. While looping behind the Moon, the crew reached a distance of nearly 249,000 miles from Earth, farther than any humans had ever traveled, a record that still stands. They had little time to enjoy it. Lovell later recalled how they barely glanced at the lunar surface sliding by below.

Surviving the days that followed was a matter of small, stubborn problems. The first was carbon dioxide. Two people's worth of air filters were meant to serve two people for two days, and now three were breathing the cabin air. The gas level climbed toward dangerous levels. The command module carried spare filters, but they were square, and the lunar module's receptacles were round. On the ground, engineers gathered the same items the crew had on board, such as plastic bags, cardboard, a sock, and duct tape, and worked out how to fit one to the other. They read the instructions to the astronauts over the radio, and the crew built the improvised adapter. The gas level fell.

The second problem was cold. With most systems off to save power, the cabin temperature dropped to near freezing. The men wore their flight suits and whatever else they could find, and slept poorly. Water was rationed to a few ounces a day, which left them dehydrated. Haise developed a fever and a urinary infection. Condensation dripped from the walls. Lovell lost about 14 pounds over the flight, and the three men lost nearly 30 pounds between them.

The third problem was navigation. Without the normal systems running, the crew had to correct their course by hand. Their trajectory was drifting, and a small error could mean skipping off the atmosphere or burning up. At one point they used the Earth itself as a reference, lining up the planet's sunlit edge in a window to hold the ship's orientation during a burn. All of it was done in a cold, cramped cabin by tired men.

Meanwhile, a team on the ground worked on how to restart Odyssey. The ship had been built to run for days on its fuel cells, not to be revived from a cold start on battery power alone. Engineers developed a new sequence that would bring the systems back one at a time without draining the limited supply. Mattingly, who had been grounded and who felt the loss keenly, spent long hours in a simulator testing each step and helping refine the procedure. When the time came, the crew would follow it line by line.

On April 17, the final day, the astronauts separated from the dead service module. As it drifted away, they saw that an entire panel on the side had been blown off, and the damage was far worse than anyone had expected. Then they powered up Odyssey and said goodbye to Aquarius, the little craft that had saved them. It was released shortly before reentry.

The last uncertainty came during reentry. The heat of the atmosphere ionizes the air around a spacecraft and blocks radio signals, and it normally lasts about three minutes. This time, the silence stretched past that. Mission Control waited. Millions of people watching at home waited. Then the voice of Swigert came through the static, and on the television screens parachutes bloomed against the sky.

Odyssey splashed down in the South Pacific near Samoa, within sight of the recovery ship USS Iwo Jima, a little under 143 hours after launch. The crew was weak, thin, and dehydrated, but all three were alive. Apollo 13 never reached the Moon. In the years since, many people have come to see it as NASA's finest hour, a reminder that a spacecraft's most valuable component may be the people who think their way out of trouble, both in the cabin and on the ground.
